102748.q: What is a pharmacy called that also helps at night or on Sundays?
102748.e: An emergency pharmacy is available outside normal opening hours too. That way you can get urgently needed medicines even at night.
102748.m: The emergency pharmacy helps at night and on Sundays too.

102749.q: What can you buy at the pharmacy without a prescription?
102749.e: Plasters, creams for insect bites and some simple remedies are available without a prescription. The pharmacist gives you advice.
102749.m: You can get plasters at the pharmacy without a prescription.

102750.q: What does the expiry date on a medicine show?
102750.e: After the expiry date, a medicine may no longer work properly. Out-of-date medicines are taken back to the pharmacy.
102750.m: Out-of-date medicines go back to the pharmacy.

102751.q: Why do children often get an injection at the doctor’s?
102751.e: Many vaccinations are given with an injection. The prick is short and then often protects you for many years.
102751.m: A vaccination is often given as an injection.

102752.q: Where is a vaccination injection usually given?
102752.e: Most vaccines are injected into the muscle of the upper arm. For babies, the thigh is often used.
102752.m: Vaccine injections are usually given in the upper arm.

102753.q: What does the nurse do to the skin before an injection?
102753.e: A swab with disinfectant removes the germs from the skin. That way no germs get into the body with the needle.
102753.m: Before an injection, the skin is disinfected.

102754.q: What is often stuck on the spot after an injection?
102754.e: A small plaster protects the spot until the tiny prick has healed. Often it only bleeds a tiny bit.
102754.m: A plaster goes on the injection spot.

102755.q: What can help if you are scared of an injection?
102755.e: Calm breathing helps you relax. A loose arm hurts less than a tense one.
102755.m: Calm breathing helps against fear of injections.

102756.q: What is at the front of a syringe?
102756.e: At the front of the syringe there is a very thin needle. The medicine flows through it into the body.
102756.m: A syringe has a thin needle at the front.

102757.q: What is taken out of the body with the needle during a blood test?
102757.e: The blood goes into a small tube. It is examined in the laboratory so the doctor can learn more about your health.
102757.m: For a blood test, a little blood is examined.

102758.q: What is the hospital department called that you go to straight away after an accident?
102758.e: In accident and emergency, injured people and people who suddenly become seriously ill are treated at once. Specialists who know all about emergencies work there.
102758.m: Accident and emergency helps immediately after accidents.

102759.q: What do you call a doctor who comes straight to an accident with the ambulance or helicopter?
102759.e: The emergency doctor treats injured people at the scene of the accident. Afterwards they are taken to hospital.
102759.m: The emergency doctor helps right at the scene of the accident.

102760.q: What is the vehicle called that takes sick and injured people quickly to hospital?
102760.e: In Switzerland it is also usually called an ambulance (Ambulanz). It takes sick and injured people to hospital quickly.
102760.m: An ambulance takes people quickly to hospital.

102761.q: Where do very seriously ill people go who have to be watched all the time?
102761.e: In intensive care, the heart, breathing and other values are monitored round the clock. Especially many specialists work there for each patient.
102761.m: In intensive care, seriously ill people are monitored constantly.

102762.q: How does Rega quickly rescue injured people from the mountains?
102762.e: Rega flies helicopters to accidents, including in the mountains. That way injured people get to hospital quickly.
102762.m: Rega flies helicopters to injured people.

102763.q: Who is treated first in accident and emergency?
102763.e: In accident and emergency, staff check how urgently someone needs help. Anyone whose life is in danger goes first, even if others have been waiting longer.
102763.m: In A&E, the most urgent cases go first.

102764.q: What colour are operating clothes often?
102764.e: Green and blue are restful for the eyes when you look at red for a long time. That is why many operating clothes are green or blue.
102764.m: Operating clothes are often green or blue.

102765.q: What is the sport called where you throw a ball into a basket from a wheelchair?
102765.e: In wheelchair basketball the basket is the same height as in normal basketball. It is a sport at the Paralympics.
102765.m: In wheelchair basketball you throw the ball into a basket.

102766.q: What do you call a doctor who carries out operations?
102766.e: Surgeons operate. They treat illnesses and injuries with fine instruments.

102767.q: What is the room called where operations take place?
102767.e: The operating theatre is especially clean and bright. All the equipment needed for an operation is there.
102767.m: Operations take place in the operating theatre.

102768.q: Why does the operating team wear a mask over mouth and nose?
a: So no germs get into the wound
102768.e: When you speak and breathe, tiny droplets come out of your mouth. The mask holds them back so the open wound stays clean.
102768.m: The mask in the operating theatre keeps germs away from the wound.

102769.q: What does the operating team wear on their hands?
102769.e: The gloves are sterile and only used once. Jewellery is taken off before an operation.
102769.m: During an operation you wear sterile gloves.

102770.q: What does the surgeon do with the cut in the skin at the end of an operation?
102770.e: The wound is closed with stitches, clips or glue. That way it can heal well.
102770.m: After the operation, the wound is closed.

102771.q: Where in the tummy does it often hurt with appendicitis?
a: Right at the top under the ribs
102771.e: The appendix is in the bottom right of the tummy. If it is inflamed, it often hurts there and you need an operation.
102771.m: An inflamed appendix hurts in the bottom right of the tummy.

102772.q: What does “sterile” mean for instruments used in an operation?
102772.e: Sterile instruments are made germ-free with great heat or in other ways. That way no germs get into the wound during the operation.

102773.q: What is the small, very sharp knife used for operating called?
102773.e: With the scalpel the surgeon makes fine, precise cuts. It is sharper than any kitchen knife.
102773.m: The knife for operating is called a scalpel.

102774.q: What happens under a general anaesthetic?
a: You sleep deeply and feel nothing
102774.e: Under a general anaesthetic you sleep very deeply. So you feel no pain from the operation and notice nothing.
102774.m: Under a general anaesthetic you sleep and feel no pain.

102775.q: Who makes sure during an operation that you sleep deeply and feel nothing?
102775.e: The anaesthetist gives the anaesthetic. She stays close by during the whole operation and looks after you.
102775.m: The anaesthetist looks after you during the operation.

102776.q: What are you not allowed to do for a few hours before an anaesthetic?
102776.e: Before an anaesthetic your stomach must be empty, so you must not have eaten. That way no food can get from the stomach into the lungs during the anaesthetic.
102776.m: Before an anaesthetic your stomach must be empty.

102777.q: What is it called when only a small area is made pain-free, for example at the dentist?
102777.e: With a local anaesthetic only one area becomes numb. You stay awake but feel no pain there.
102777.m: With a local anaesthetic you stay awake.

102778.q: In which room do you wake up after an operation with an anaesthetic?
102778.e: In the recovery room you are watched closely until you are fully awake again. Then you go to your ward room.
102778.m: After the anaesthetic you wake up in the recovery room.

102779.q: How do children often receive the anaesthetic?
102779.e: Children often breathe in the anaesthetic through a mask. Sometimes they get it through a thin tube into a vein.
102779.m: Children often breathe in the anaesthetic through a mask.

102780.q: What does the anaesthetist monitor during an operation?
102780.e: Machines constantly show how the heart is beating and how well you are breathing. That way anyone notices at once if something is wrong.
102780.m: During the anaesthetic, heart and breathing are monitored.

102781.q: How do you often feel right after waking up from an anaesthetic?
102781.e: The anaesthetic needs some time to leave the body. That is why you are often still tired and a little confused afterwards.
102781.m: After an anaesthetic you are often still tired.

102782.q: What is a hospital called that only treats children and teenagers?
102782.e: In a children’s hospital everything is set up for children. The doctors and nurses are also specialised in children.
102782.m: Children are treated in a children’s hospital.

102783.q: What do many people call the Children’s Hospital Zurich for short?
102783.e: The University Children’s Hospital Zurich is often simply called “Kispi”. It is one of the largest children’s hospitals in Switzerland.
102783.m: The Children’s Hospital Zurich is called Kispi for short.

102784.q: Who cares for the sick children in a children’s hospital?
102784.e: In the children’s hospital, nurses look after the sick children day and night. They work closely with the doctors.
102784.m: In the children’s hospital, nurses care for the children.

102785.q: What do large children’s hospitals have for children who must stay a long time?
102785.e: In the hospital school children keep learning so they don’t miss too much at school. The lessons are adapted to their illness.
102785.m: In the hospital school, sick children keep learning.

102786.q: Can parents stay with their child in a children’s hospital?
102786.e: For sick children it is important that mum or dad is there. That is why parents can often even sleep in the room.
102786.m: Parents can often stay with their sick child.

102787.q: What do you call a doctor who especially treats children?
102787.e: A paediatrician knows all about illnesses in babies and children. The technical word for children’s medicine is paediatrics.

102788.q: What do many children’s wards have so children can take their mind off things?
102788.e: In the playroom there are games, books and craft things. There children can forget for a while that they are ill.
102788.m: In the playroom, sick children can play.

102789.q: What can children often bring to hospital to feel more comfortable?
102789.e: A familiar cuddly toy gives comfort and security. Pets are usually not allowed in hospital for reasons of hygiene.
102789.m: A cuddly toy helps against homesickness in hospital.

102790.q: How many large drive wheels does a normal wheelchair have?
102790.e: A normal wheelchair has two large wheels at the back to push it along. At the front it has two small wheels for steering.
102790.m: A wheelchair has two large drive wheels.

102791.q: What helps people in a wheelchair get over a step?
102791.e: A ramp is a sloping surface instead of a step. You can roll up and down it in a wheelchair.
102791.m: A ramp makes steps passable for wheelchairs.

102792.q: How do you move a wheelchair without a motor forwards?
a: With your hands on the large wheels
With a crank on the seat
102792.e: A ring, the push rim, is fixed to the large wheel. You hold it with your hands and push the wheelchair forwards.
102792.m: You drive a wheelchair with your hands on the large wheels.

102793.q: What is the name of the famous Swiss wheelchair athlete nicknamed “Silver Bullet”?
102793.e: Marcel Hug is a wheelchair athlete from Thurgau. He has already won several gold medals at the Paralympic Games.
102793.m: Marcel Hug is a successful Swiss wheelchair athlete.

102794.q: What are the big sports games for athletes with disabilities called?
102794.e: Like the Olympic Games, the Paralympics take place every four years. There are wheelchair races there, for example.
102794.m: People with disabilities compete at the Paralympics.

102795.q: In which village in the canton of Lucerne is the Swiss Paraplegic Centre?
102795.e: The Swiss Paraplegic Centre in Nottwil treats people with paraplegia. Many learn there how to manage their everyday life in a wheelchair.
102795.m: The Paraplegic Centre is in Nottwil.

102796.e: An electric wheelchair has an electric motor and a battery. It is usually steered with a small joystick.
102796.m: An electric wheelchair runs on a motor and a battery.

102797.q: What background colour does the wheelchair sign on parking spaces usually have?
102797.e: The international sign shows a white wheelchair on a blue background. It marks parking spaces, toilets and entrances for wheelchair users.
102797.m: The wheelchair sign is white on a blue background.

102798.q: When do you often need crutches?
102798.e: With crutches you put less weight on the injured leg. That helps it heal better.
102798.m: Crutches take the weight off an injured leg.

102799.q: How many crutches do people usually use?
102799.e: Usually you walk with two crutches, one in each hand. That is safer and spreads your weight well.
102799.m: Usually you walk with two crutches.

102800.q: Where do you support yourself with forearm crutches?
102800.e: You hold the grip with your hand and your forearm rests in a cuff. That is where the name forearm crutch comes from.
102800.m: With forearm crutches you lean on your hands and forearms.

102801.q: What do you often get around your leg when a bone is broken?
102801.e: The cast goes hard and keeps the broken bone still. That way it can grow back together in the right position.
102801.m: A cast keeps a broken bone still.

102802.q: What does a crutch have at the bottom so it doesn’t slip?
102802.e: The rubber tip at the bottom grips the floor well. When it is worn out, it should be replaced.
102802.m: The rubber tip stops the crutch slipping.

102803.q: When climbing stairs on crutches, which leg goes onto the step first?
102803.e: Going up, the healthy leg leads because it has to lift the body. The crutches and the injured leg follow.
102803.m: Going upstairs, the healthy leg goes first.

102804.q: How do you adjust crutches to a person’s height?
102804.e: Crutches have holes and a button that let you set the length. The grips should be roughly at wrist height.
102804.m: Crutches can be adjusted in length.

102805.q: Who often shows you how to walk properly with crutches?
102805.e: The physiotherapist helps people move well again after injuries. She also practises walking with crutches.
102805.m: The physiotherapist practises walking with crutches.

102806.q: What does a hospital bed have underneath so it can be pushed?
102806.e: Hospital beds have wheels underneath. That way patients can be wheeled in their bed to examinations.
102806.m: Hospital beds have wheels for pushing.

102807.q: What can you adjust with buttons on a hospital bed?
102807.e: A motor raises and lowers the bed. The head end can also be raised so you can sit comfortably.
102807.m: On a hospital bed, height and backrest can be adjusted.

102808.q: What do you press in a hospital bed when you need help from the nurses?
102808.e: There is a call button by the bed. When you press it, the nurses know you need help.
102808.m: You call the nurses with the call button.

102809.q: Why does a hospital bed often have rails at the side?
102809.e: The side rails protect you from falling out of bed. That is important after an anaesthetic or at night, for example.
102809.m: Side rails stop you falling out.

102810.q: What stands next to the hospital bed for your drinking bottle, book and glasses?
102810.e: On the bedside table you have the most important things within reach. Often you can fold out a tray and eat at it.
102810.m: Things within reach go on the bedside table.

102811.q: Why can a hospital bed be raised?
a: So the nurses can work without hurting their backs
So you can look out of the window
102811.e: At the right height the nurse doesn’t have to bend down so far. That protects her back.
102811.m: A raised bed protects the nurses’ backs.

102812.q: What often hangs on a stand next to the bed and puts fluid into a vein?
102812.e: With a drip, fluid drips slowly through a thin tube into a vein. That way you get water or medicine.
102812.m: A drip slowly puts fluid into a vein.

102813.q: Why do the wheels of a hospital bed have brakes?
a: So the bed doesn’t roll away
102813.e: When the bed is standing in the room, the wheels are locked. That way it doesn’t roll away when someone gets in or out.
102813.m: Locked wheels hold the hospital bed in place.

102814.q: What is special about a university hospital?
a: It is only open at night
102814.e: At a university hospital, medical students learn from experienced doctors. A lot of research is also done there.
102814.m: Doctors are trained at a university hospital.

102815.q: What does the nurse bring to the patients’ beds at set times?
102815.e: The nurses make sure everyone gets the right medicine at the right time. This is set out exactly in the doctor’s plan.
102815.m: The nurses bring the medicines at the right time.

102816.q: What helps wheelchair users in a building with several floors?
102816.e: With a lift you can reach every floor without stairs. That is why public buildings need lifts.
102816.m: A lift takes a wheelchair to every floor.

102817.q: On what are injured people pushed lying down into the ambulance?
102817.e: The stretcher often has wheels and straps. That way injured people can be carried safely lying down.
102817.m: Injured people are carried lying down on a stretcher.

103110.q: What do you call tiny living things and particles that can make us ill?
103110.e: Germs, or pathogens, can get into the body through the mouth, nose or small wounds. There they multiply and make us ill.
103110.m: Germs are tiny and can make us ill.

103111.q: Can you see germs with the naked eye?
103111.e: Most germs are much smaller than a grain of sand. You need a microscope to see them.

103112.q: How long should you rub your hands with soap?
103112.e: The soap needs some time to loosen dirt and germs. You also rub between your fingers and under your nails.
103112.m: Thorough handwashing takes at least 20 seconds.

103113.q: Which kinds of germs are there, for example?
103113.e: Pathogens are mainly bacteria, viruses and some fungi. Some worms can also make you ill.
103113.m: Bacteria, viruses and fungi can cause illnesses.

103114.q: Where in the kitchen do especially many germs often live?
103114.e: A washing-up sponge is damp, warm and full of food scraps. Bacteria multiply very well there, so you change it often.
103114.m: You should change a washing-up sponge often.

103115.q: Why don’t you cut raw meat and salad on the same board?
a: Germs can get onto the salad
103115.e: There can be germs on raw meat. The salad is not cooked, so these germs would not be killed.
103115.m: Use a separate chopping board for raw meat.

103116.e: After the toilet there can be germs from the gut on your hands. Soap washes them away.
103116.m: Always wash your hands after the toilet.

103117.q: What helps the body defend itself well against germs?
a: Watching TV for a long time
103117.e: If you sleep well, move and eat healthily, you strengthen your defences. Then your body can fight germs better.
103117.m: Sleep and healthy food strengthen your defences.

103118.q: Which common illness with a runny nose, sore throat and cough is usually caused by viruses?
103118.e: A cold is usually caused by viruses, for example rhinoviruses. It is usually over after about a week.
103118.m: A cold usually comes from viruses.

103119.q: Which illness is caused by a virus?
103119.e: Real flu is caused by the influenza virus. Tooth decay, on the other hand, is caused by bacteria in the mouth.

103120.q: Can you see viruses with the naked eye?
a: No, they are far too small
Yes, they are as big as grains of sand
103120.e: Viruses are tiny, much smaller than a grain of sand. You can only see them with very special microscopes.
103120.m: Viruses are far too small to see.

103121.q: Which illness did the coronavirus cause around the world from 2020?
103121.e: A new coronavirus spread worldwide from early 2020. The illness it causes is called Covid-19.
103121.m: Covid-19 is caused by a coronavirus.

103122.e: Chickenpox is caused by the varicella-zoster virus. Itchy blisters all over the body are typical.

103123.q: Why can you catch flu again and again?
a: Flu only comes from the weather
103123.e: Flu viruses keep changing a little. That is why the body’s defences don’t always recognise them again.

103124.q: What often grows on old bread as green or white fluff?
103124.e: Mould often grows on old, damp bread. It looks like a fluffy coating.
103124.m: Fluff on old bread is usually mould.

103125.q: What does mould especially need to grow?
103125.e: Moulds grow best where it is damp and warm. In the fridge they grow more slowly.
103125.m: Mould likes it damp and warm.

103126.q: What do you do with a mouldy loaf of bread?
103126.e: The fine threads of mould often grow invisibly deep into the bread. That is why you throw the whole loaf away.
103126.m: Mouldy bread belongs entirely in the bin.

a: Through tiny spores in the air
103127.e: Moulds form tiny spores. These fly through the air and grow wherever it is damp.
103127.m: Mould spreads through the air with spores.

103128.q: Which medicine was obtained from a mould?
103128.e: In 1928 Alexander Fleming discovered that a mould kills bacteria. Penicillin was made from it.

103129.q: Which cheese deliberately has a white mould on the outside?
103129.e: On Camembert, an edible white mould grows on the rind. It gives the cheese its flavour.
103129.m: Camembert has an edible white mould.

103130.q: What helps against mould on the walls of a flat?
103130.e: When you air the rooms, damp air goes out. Without much damp, mould can hardly grow on the walls.

103131.q: Which group of living things does mould belong to?
103131.e: Mould is a fungus. It is made of fine threads and forms spores.

103132.q: Why shouldn’t you sniff mouldy food?
103132.e: When you sniff, mould spores get into your nose and lungs. That can be unhealthy and trigger allergies.

103134.q: What does the body learn from a vaccination?
103134.e: A vaccination shows the body a harmless part of a germ. That way the defences learn to recognise and fight the real germ quickly.
103134.m: A vaccination trains the body’s defences.

103135.q: Where are a child’s vaccinations recorded?
103135.e: The vaccination record shows which vaccinations you had and when. That way the doctor knows what is still missing.
103135.m: The vaccination record shows all vaccinations.

103136.q: What do you call a vaccination that strengthens protection again after a few years?
103136.e: With some vaccinations, for example against tetanus, the protection fades over time. A booster makes it strong again.
103136.m: A booster strengthens vaccine protection again.

103137.q: Which disease no longer exists in the world thanks to vaccinations?
103137.e: Smallpox was defeated with worldwide vaccinations. In 1980 the World Health Organization declared it wiped out.
103137.m: Smallpox was wiped out thanks to vaccinations.

103138.q: Which three diseases does the MMR vaccine protect against?
103138.e: The MMR vaccine is a triple vaccine. The three letters stand for the first letters of the three childhood diseases.
103138.m: The MMR vaccine protects against three childhood diseases.

103139.q: Which disease from tick bites can you be vaccinated against?
103139.e: TBE is an inflammation of the brain and its lining that is passed on by ticks. This vaccination is recommended in large parts of Switzerland.
103139.m: There is a vaccine against the tick disease TBE.

103140.q: What can happen for a short time after a vaccination?
103140.e: The injection spot can be a bit red or sore for one or two days. Sometimes you also get a slight temperature.
103140.m: After a vaccination your arm can hurt for a short time.

103141.q: Which disease, also known as polio, are children vaccinated against today?
103141.e: Infantile paralysis, also called polio, is caused by a virus and can paralyse muscles. Thanks to vaccinations it hardly occurs in Europe any more.

103142.q: How does a vaccination also protect other people?
103142.e: If you are vaccinated, you get ill less often and pass on germs less often. That way babies and sick people are also better protected.
103142.m: Vaccination also protects the people around us.

103143.e: Measles is caused by the measles virus. It gets into the body when you breathe.
103143.m: Measles is caused by a virus.

103144.q: What do you see on the skin with measles?
103144.e: After a few days you get red spots that often start behind the ears and on the face. Then they spread over the whole body.

103145.e: Measles is one of the most contagious diseases of all. Almost every unprotected person who comes into contact with the virus becomes ill.

103146.q: How is the measles virus usually passed on?
103146.e: When people cough, sneeze or talk, tiny droplets with the virus get into the air. Anyone who breathes them in can be infected.

103147.q: Which symptoms do you often have at the start of measles?
103147.e: Measles starts like a bad cold with fever, a runny nose and a cough. The eyes are often red too.
103147.m: Measles starts with fever and a cough.

103148.q: How many times in your life do you usually get measles?
103148.e: Anyone who has had measles is usually protected for life afterwards. The body remembers the virus.
103148.m: After measles you are usually protected for good.

103149.q: How many doses of measles vaccine does the Swiss vaccination plan recommend?
103149.e: For safe protection you need two vaccinations. In Switzerland, young children get them in their first and second year of life.
103149.m: For protection against measles you need two vaccinations.

a: Yes, it only lasts an hour
Yes, you don’t notice it at all
103150.e: Measles can lead to pneumonia or inflammation of the brain. That is why protection through vaccination is important.

103151.q: What does a child with mumps often look like?
a: With red spots all over the body
103151.e: With mumps, the salivary glands in front of the ears swell up. The face then looks like a hamster with full cheeks.

103152.q: Which gland swells up with mumps?
103152.e: The parotid gland is in front of and below the ear. It makes saliva and becomes swollen and painful with mumps.
103152.m: With mumps, the parotid gland swells up.

103154.e: The mumps virus is in saliva. It can be passed on by coughing, sneezing, a kiss on the cheek or sharing a glass.
103154.m: Mumps is passed on through saliva.

103155.q: Besides swollen cheeks, what else do you often have with mumps?
103155.e: Many children with mumps have a fever and a headache and feel weak. Chewing can hurt too.
103155.m: Mumps often comes with fever and a headache.

103156.q: How common is mumps in Switzerland today compared with the past?
103156.e: Since there has been a vaccine, far fewer children catch mumps. In the past almost every child got this illness.
103156.m: Thanks to vaccination, mumps has become rare.

103157.q: What should a child with mumps do?
103157.e: Mumps is contagious. If you are ill, you rest at home so you don’t infect anyone.
103157.m: With mumps you stay at home.

103158.e: Mumps is caused by the mumps virus and passes from person to person. It is a typical childhood illness.
103158.m: Mumps is a contagious viral illness.

103159.q: What do you see on the skin with rubella?
103159.e: With rubella, small light red spots appear on the skin. They usually only itch a little.

103160.q: Where does the rubella rash usually start?
103160.e: The rash usually starts on the face and behind the ears. Then it spreads over the body.
103160.m: The rubella rash starts on the face.

103161.q: What often swells up with rubella?
a: The lymph nodes in the neck
103161.e: With rubella, the lymph nodes in the neck and behind the ears get swollen. They are part of the body’s defences.
103161.m: With rubella, the lymph nodes in the neck swell up.

103162.q: How serious is rubella in children usually?
103162.e: In children, rubella is usually a mild illness. Many only have a slight fever and a rash.
103162.m: Rubella is usually mild in children.

103164.e: Rubella is caused by the rubella virus. It is passed on by coughing and talking.
103164.m: Rubella is caused by a virus.

103165.q: How long does the rubella rash usually last?
103165.e: The rubella rash usually disappears after one to three days. It leaves no scars.
103165.m: The rubella rash disappears after a few days.

103166.q: Does every child notice when they have rubella?
103166.e: Many rubella infections pass without clear signs. You can still pass the virus on.
103166.m: You can have rubella without noticing.

103167.e: Whooping cough is caused by the bacterium Bordetella pertussis. It settles in the airways.
103167.m: Whooping cough is caused by bacteria.

103168.q: What is typical of whooping cough?
103168.e: With whooping cough you get violent coughing fits. You cough many times in a row.
103168.m: Whooping cough causes strong coughing fits.

103169.q: What sound do you hear after a coughing fit with whooping cough?
a: A drawn-out gasp when breathing in
A loud whistle when breathing out
103169.e: After the coughing fit, you draw in air with a gasping, whooping sound. That is where the illness gets its name.
103169.m: With whooping cough you gasp in air after coughing.

103170.q: How long does whooping cough often last?
103170.e: The cough with whooping cough can last many weeks. In China it is even called the “hundred-day cough”.
103170.m: Whooping cough often lasts many weeks.

103171.q: Who is whooping cough especially dangerous for?
103171.e: Babies with whooping cough can stop breathing for short moments. That is why the people around them should protect themselves too.
103171.m: Whooping cough is especially dangerous for babies.

103172.q: How is whooping cough passed on?
103172.e: When people cough and sneeze, tiny droplets with the bacteria fly through the air. Others breathe them in.

103173.e: There is a vaccine against whooping cough. The Swiss vaccination plan recommends it for babies already.
103173.m: A vaccination protects against whooping cough.

103174.q: When do the coughing fits of whooping cough often come especially often?
103174.e: With whooping cough, the coughing fits are often especially strong at night. That is why sick children sleep badly.

103175.q: Which parts of a microscope make the image bigger?
103175.e: A microscope contains several glass lenses. They bend the light so that small things look big.
103175.m: Glass lenses in the microscope make the image bigger.

103176.q: What is the small glass plate called that you put the sample on for a microscope?
103176.e: The sample goes on a thin glass slide. Often a cover slip is placed on top.
103176.m: The sample lies on a slide.

103177.q: What is the part of the microscope you look into called?
103177.e: The eyepiece is the lens you hold your eye to. Its technical name, ocular, comes from the Latin “oculus”, eye.
103177.m: You look into the microscope through the eyepiece.

103178.q: Who was one of the first people to see bacteria, around 1676, with a microscope he built himself?
103178.e: The Dutchman Antonie van Leeuwenhoek made tiny, very powerful lenses. With them he discovered small living things that he called “little animals”.
103178.m: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek discovered bacteria with the microscope.

103179.q: Which device magnifies less than a microscope?
103179.e: A magnifying glass is a single lens and only magnifies a few times. A microscope magnifies much more.
103179.m: A magnifying glass magnifies less than a microscope.

103180.q: The eyepiece magnifies 10 times and the objective lens also 10 times. How much does the microscope magnify?
103180.e: You multiply the two magnifications: 10 times 10 makes 100. So the image is 100 times bigger.
103180.m: The magnifications of eyepiece and objective are multiplied.

103181.q: Where does the light usually come from on a school microscope?
a: From above out of the eyepiece
From the side through the window
103181.e: There is a lamp under the stage of the microscope. Its light shines up through the thin sample into your eye.
103181.m: On a school microscope, light shines from below through the sample.

103182.q: What do you see under the microscope in a drop of pond water?
103182.e: Countless tiny living things such as slipper animalcules and algae live in pond water. With a microscope you can see them swimming around.
103182.m: Tiny living things live in a drop of pond water.

103183.q: What do you use to bring the image into focus on a microscope?
103183.e: There are focus knobs on the stand of the microscope. When you turn them, the stage moves until the image is sharp.
103183.m: You focus the image with the focus knob.

103185.q: Which illness do you often catch when someone coughs on you?
103185.e: When someone coughs, tiny droplets with germs fly through the air. Anyone who breathes them in can catch a cold.
103185.m: Cold germs fly through the air when people cough.

103186.q: What do you call infection through hands and objects?
103186.e: Germs can sit on door handles, toys and hands. If you then touch your mouth, nose or eyes, you become infected.
103186.m: You can also be infected through hands and objects.

103188.q: Why is it better not to touch your eyes, nose and mouth often?
a: Germs get into the body that way
103188.e: There are often germs on your hands. They can easily get into the body through the eyes, nose and mouth.
103188.m: Don’t touch your face with unwashed hands.

103189.q: What does it mean if an illness is contagious?
a: It can pass to other people
It only lasts a short time
103189.e: A contagious illness is caused by germs. These can travel from one person to the next.
103189.m: Contagious illnesses pass to other people.

103190.q: Which of these complaints is not contagious?
103190.e: Sunburn is caused by too much sun on the skin. It is not caused by germs and cannot be passed on.

103191.q: Why don’t you drink from the same bottle as a friend who is ill?
103191.e: Saliva with germs stays on the neck of the bottle. Whoever drinks next can be infected.
103191.m: Don’t share a drinking bottle with someone who is ill.

103192.e: Hay fever is an allergy and is not caused by germs. That is why you cannot infect anyone with it.

103193.q: When do many people have hay fever?
103193.e: In spring and summer, trees, grasses and herbs flower. Then especially large amounts of pollen fly through the air.
103193.m: Hay fever comes mainly in spring and summer.

103194.q: The pollen of which tree often causes hay fever in Switzerland?
103194.e: Birch pollen is one of the most common causes of hay fever. Birch trees usually flower in April.
103194.m: Birch pollen often causes hay fever.

103195.q: What often happens to your eyes with hay fever?
103195.e: The pollen irritates the eyes. The defences react, and the eyes go red, itch and water.
103195.m: With hay fever your eyes often itch.

103196.q: What happens in the body with an allergy?
103196.e: With an allergy, the defences think harmless substances such as pollen are dangerous. They fight back too strongly.
103196.m: With an allergy, the defences react too strongly.

103197.q: Which shrub flowers in winter and can cause hay fever early?
103197.e: Hazel often flowers as early as January or February. Its yellow catkins then release lots of pollen.

103198.q: What helps with hay fever in the evening?
103198.e: During the day lots of pollen gets caught in your hair. If you wash it in the evening, less pollen gets into your bed.
103198.m: Washing your hair in the evening keeps pollen out of bed.

103199.q: Who publishes pollen forecasts in Switzerland?
103199.e: MeteoSwiss measures in many places how much pollen is in the air. That way people with allergies can prepare for high pollen counts.

103200.q: What forms in the mouth with hand, foot and mouth disease?
103200.e: Small blisters that can hurt appear in the mouth. There are also spots and blisters on the hands and feet.
103200.m: With this illness you have blisters in your mouth.

103201.q: What causes hand, foot and mouth disease?
103201.e: The illness is caused by certain viruses called enteroviruses. It passes from person to person.
103201.m: Hand, foot and mouth disease is caused by viruses.

103202.q: Who gets hand, foot and mouth disease most often?
103202.e: Mainly children under ten catch it, often at nursery and kindergarten. Adults are usually already protected.
103202.m: Mainly young children get hand, foot and mouth disease.

103203.q: How does hand, foot and mouth disease usually go?
a: Harmlessly, better after about a week
Always with a stay in hospital
103203.e: The illness usually heals by itself after seven to ten days. Serious cases are rare.
103203.m: Hand, foot and mouth disease usually heals by itself.

103204.q: Why do children with hand, foot and mouth disease often eat badly?
a: The blisters in the mouth hurt
103204.e: The blisters in the mouth hurt when chewing and swallowing. Cool, soft food and lots to drink help.
103204.m: Cool, soft food helps with blisters in the mouth.

103205.q: What protects well against hand, foot and mouth disease?
103205.e: The viruses are in saliva, in the blisters and in poo. Frequent handwashing stops them being passed on.
103205.m: Handwashing protects against hand, foot and mouth disease.

103206.q: Where do you get spots and blisters with hand, foot and mouth disease?
a: On the hands, feet and in the mouth
103206.e: The name gives it away: the spots and blisters appear on the hands, on the feet and in the mouth.
103206.m: The blisters appear on the hands, feet and in the mouth.

103207.q: How does hand, foot and mouth disease often start?
a: With a fever and a sore throat
103207.e: At first you often have a slight fever, a sore throat and little appetite. One or two days later the blisters come.
103207.m: Hand, foot and mouth disease often starts with a fever.

103500.q: What is the smallest bone in the human body called?
103500.e: The stirrup is only a few millimetres long. No other bone in the body is smaller.
103500.m: The stirrup is the smallest bone in the body.

103501.q: About how big is the stirrup bone in the ear?
103501.e: The stirrup measures only about 3 millimetres. It fits easily on a fingertip.
103501.m: The stirrup is only about 3 millimetres long.

103502.q: Which bone is one of the tiny ear bones?
103502.e: There are tiny ear bones in the middle ear. One of them is called the anvil, like the blacksmith’s tool.
103502.m: The anvil is one of the ear bones.

103503.q: What is the stirrup bone in the ear named after?
a: A foot holder used in riding
103503.e: A stirrup hangs from the saddle and holds the rider’s foot. The bone in the ear looks just like it.
103503.m: The stirrup bone is named after the foot holder on a saddle.

103504.q: What do the tiny bones in the ear help with?
103504.e: The bones pass on the vibrations from the eardrum. That is how you can hear sounds.
103504.m: The ear bones help us hear.

103505.q: What is the smallest muscle in the human body called?
103505.e: This tiny muscle is attached to a bone in the ear. It protects the ear from very loud noises.
103505.m: The smallest muscle is the stapedius.

103506.q: Where are more than half of all bones?
103506.e: Hands and feet have lots of small bones. Together they make up more than half of all bones.
103506.m: More than half of our bones are in our hands and feet.

103507.q: How many bones does a hand including the wrist have?
103507.e: The fingers, palm and wrist have 27 bones altogether. That is why the hand is so flexible.
103507.m: A hand with its wrist has 27 bones.

103508.q: About how many hairs does a person have on their head?
103508.e: About 100,000 hairs grow on the head. Fair-haired people often have a few more.
103508.m: About 100,000 hairs grow on the head.

103509.q: How many hairs from your head do you normally lose in a day?
103509.e: About 50 to 100 hairs fall out every day. That is normal, because new hairs grow back.
103509.m: You lose about 50 to 100 hairs every day.

103510.q: What is hair mainly made of?
103510.e: Hair is mainly made of keratin, a horny substance. Nails are made of the same material.
103510.m: Hair is made of keratin, a horny substance.

103511.q: Why does hair go grey in old age?
103511.e: In old age the hair root makes less pigment. Without pigment, hair looks grey or white.
103511.m: Grey hair has too little pigment.

103512.q: Does a child’s heart beat faster or slower than an adult’s?
103512.e: Children have a smaller heart. That is why it has to beat more often than an adult’s heart.

103513.q: About how long are all the blood vessels of an adult put together?
103513.e: If you laid all the blood vessels end to end, they would be about 100,000 kilometres long. Most of them are tiny and thin.
103513.m: All blood vessels together are about 100,000 kilometres long.

103514.q: About how many times would all of a person’s blood vessels go round the Earth?
a: About two and a half times
Only a tenth of the way
103514.e: The Earth’s circumference at the equator is about 40,000 kilometres. So about 100,000 kilometres of blood vessels would go round about two and a half times.
103514.m: A person’s blood vessels would go round the Earth about two and a half times.

103516.q: About how heavy is an adult’s skin?
103516.e: An adult’s skin weighs several kilograms. Depending on whether you count the layer under the skin, it is about 3 to 10 kilograms.

103517.q: About how large is the area of an adult’s skin?
103517.e: If you spread the skin out, it would be about 1.5 to 2 square metres. That is as much as a big bath towel.
103517.m: An adult’s skin is about 2 square metres.

a: On the sole of the foot
103518.e: The skin on the sole of the foot is especially thick. It has to put up with a lot when you walk.
103518.m: The skin is thickest on the sole of the foot.

103519.e: The skin on the eyelid is very thin. That way you can open and close your eye easily.
103519.m: The skin is thinnest on the eyelid.

103520.q: About how often does the top layer of skin renew itself?
103520.e: Old skin flakes fall off all the time. In about four weeks the top layer is new.
103520.m: The top layer of skin renews itself about every month.

103521.q: Do your eyes move while you sleep?
103521.e: In dream sleep, the eyes move quickly back and forth under the lids. That is why this phase is called REM sleep.
103521.m: When you dream, your eyes move quickly.

103522.q: About how big is an adult’s eyeball?
103522.e: An eyeball is about 2.5 centimetres across. That is about the size of a marble or a bit bigger.
103522.m: An eyeball is about 2.5 centimetres across.

103523.q: What do your eyes do when you look to the left?
a: Both turn at the same time
103523.e: The eye muscles of both eyes work together. That way both eyes look at the same point.
103523.m: Both eyes move at the same time.

103524.q: About how long does a blink last?
103524.e: A blink is very quick. It only lasts a fraction of a second.
103524.m: A blink lasts less than half a second.

103526.q: What do you almost always do automatically when you sneeze?
103526.e: When you sneeze, your eyes close all by themselves. That is a reflex.
103526.m: When you sneeze, your eyes close by themselves.

103527.q: Can bright sunlight make some people sneeze?
103527.e: Some people have to sneeze when they suddenly look into bright light. This is called photic sneezing.
103527.m: Bright light can make some people sneeze.

103528.q: How far can droplets fly when you sneeze?
103528.e: Fine droplets can float several metres when you sneeze. That is why you should keep your distance and turn away when sneezing.
103528.m: Sneeze droplets can fly several metres.

103529.q: What is the tongue made of?
103529.e: The tongue is made of several muscles that work together. That is why it can move so well.
103529.m: The tongue is made of several muscles.

103530.q: Is the tongue the strongest muscle in the body?
a: Yes, but only in the morning
103530.e: The tongue is very flexible and works hard. But it is not the strongest muscle.
103530.m: The tongue is not the strongest muscle.

103531.q: Which taste is one of the basic tastes?
103531.e: The tongue can tell sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami apart. Dark chocolate, for example, tastes bitter.

103532.q: About how many taste buds does a person have?
103532.e: A person has about 2,000 to 5,000 taste buds, most of them on the tongue. We taste with them.
103532.m: A person has a few thousand taste buds.

103533.q: Who was the tallest person whose height was reliably measured?
103533.e: Robert Wadlow died in 1940. According to Guinness World Records he is the tallest person ever measured.
103533.m: Robert Wadlow was the tallest person ever measured.

103534.q: How tall was Robert Wadlow, the tallest person ever measured?
103534.e: Robert Wadlow grew to 2.72 metres. He needed huge, specially made shoes.

103535.q: Which country is Sultan Kösen, the tallest living man (as of 2025), from?
103535.e: Sultan Kösen comes from Turkey. According to Guinness World Records he is the tallest living man.
103535.m: Sultan Kösen from Turkey is the tallest living man.

103536.q: Why are you a little shorter in the evening than in the morning?
a: The discs in your spine get squashed
103536.e: Soft discs lie between the vertebrae. When you stand and walk, they get squashed together.
103536.m: The discs in your spine get squashed during the day.

103537.q: When does a person grow fastest?
a: In the first year of life
103537.e: In its first year a baby grows about 25 centimetres. You never grow that fast again.
103537.m: You grow fastest in your first year of life.

103538.q: About how tall was Chandra Bahadur Dangi, the shortest adult man ever measured?
103538.e: Chandra Bahadur Dangi from Nepal was 54.6 centimetres tall. He died in 2015.
103538.m: The shortest man ever measured was only about 55 centimetres tall.

103539.q: About how tall is Rumeysa Gelgi, the tallest living woman (as of 2025)?
103539.e: Rumeysa Gelgi was measured at 2.15 metres. According to Guinness World Records she is the tallest living woman.
103539.m: The tallest living woman is about 2.15 metres tall.

103540.q: About how much of an adult’s body is water?
103540.e: An adult’s body is about 60 per cent water. That is more than half.
103540.m: An adult is about 60 per cent water.

103541.q: Does a baby have more or less water in its body than an adult?
103541.e: A newborn baby is about 75 per cent water. The share goes down with age.
103541.m: Babies have more water in their bodies than adults.

103542.q: Which drink is a good and cheap thirst quencher in Switzerland?
103542.e: Tap water in Switzerland is clean and perfectly safe to drink. It has no sugar.
103542.m: Tap water is a good thirst quencher.

103543.q: Do you also lose water when you breathe out?
103543.e: Your breath contains water vapour. You can see it when you breathe on a cold window.
103543.m: When you breathe out, you lose water as water vapour.

103544.q: What does fresh sweat smell like?
103544.e: Fresh sweat is mostly water and a little salt and hardly smells. The smell only develops later on the skin.
103544.m: Fresh sweat smells of almost nothing.

103545.q: Where do you have especially many sweat glands?
a: On the palms and soles of the feet
103545.e: There are especially many sweat glands on the palms and soles. That is why they quickly get damp when you are excited.
103545.m: Palms and soles have especially many sweat glands.

103546.q: How many stirrup bones does a person have?
103546.e: There is a stirrup bone in each ear. Because we have two ears, there are two.
103546.m: Everyone has two stirrup bones, one in each ear.

103547.q: Which thin membrane in the ear is the hammer bone attached to?
103547.e: The hammer is connected to the eardrum. When the eardrum vibrates, the hammer moves too.
103547.m: The hammer is attached to the eardrum.

103548.q: About how much does the stirrup bone in the ear weigh?
103548.e: The stirrup weighs only a few milligrams. It is much lighter than a grain of rice.
103548.m: The stirrup weighs only a few milligrams.

103549.q: How many ear bones does a person have in both ears together?
103549.e: There are three ear bones in each ear. With two ears that is 3 times 2, so 6.
103549.m: Together, both ears have six ear bones.

103550.q: Which substance in the body is even harder than bone?
103550.e: Tooth enamel is the hardest substance in the whole body. It is even harder than any bone.
103550.m: Tooth enamel is harder than bone.

103551.e: Bones are made of living cells and are supplied with blood. That is why they can grow and heal.
103551.m: Bones are alive and can heal.

103552.q: Which is the longest bone in the arm?
103552.e: The humerus reaches from the shoulder to the elbow. It is the longest bone in the arm.
103552.m: The humerus is the longest bone in the arm.

103553.q: Why does a baby have soft spots on its head?
a: The skull bones have not grown together yet
The baby has no hair yet
The head is full of water
103553.e: In babies, the bones of the head have not fully grown together yet. In between there are soft spots that later become hard.
103553.m: Babies have soft spots on their heads because the bones are still growing.

103554.q: About how long does a hair on your head grow before it falls out?
103554.e: A hair on your head usually grows for several years. Then it falls out and a new one grows.
103554.m: A hair on your head grows for several years.

103555.q: About how thick is a single hair on your head?
103555.e: A hair is only about 0.05 to 0.1 millimetres thick. That is why you only see it well when it is longer.
103555.m: A hair is less than a millimetre thick.

103556.q: Does hair grow faster if you cut it often?
103556.e: Hair grows from the root under the skin. Whether you cut the ends makes no difference.
103556.m: Cutting your hair doesn’t make it grow faster.

103557.q: About how many hairs does a person have on their whole body?
103557.e: Fine little hairs grow almost everywhere on the body. Together there are several million.
103557.m: A person has several million hairs on the whole body.

103558.q: Why doesn’t having your hair cut hurt?
a: There are no nerves in hair
103558.e: There are no nerves in the hair itself. You only feel something at the root in the skin, which is why pulling hair hurts.

103559.q: A heart beats 70 times a minute. How many times does it beat in 10 minutes?
103559.e: You calculate 70 times 10. That makes 700 beats.
103559.m: At 70 beats a minute, a heart beats 700 times in 10 minutes.

103560.q: Since when does a person’s heart beat?
103560.e: The heart starts beating very early in the mother’s tummy. So it beats long before birth.
103560.m: The heart beats even before birth.

103561.q: About how much blood does the heart pump in one minute at rest?
103561.e: At rest, an adult’s heart pumps about 5 litres of blood a minute. During sport it is much more.
103561.m: At rest the heart pumps about 5 litres of blood a minute.

103562.q: About how much blood does the heart pump in a single day?
103562.e: A day has 1,440 minutes. At about 5 litres a minute, that is over 7,000 litres.
103562.m: The heart pumps over 7,000 litres of blood every day.

103563.q: About how many times does an adult’s heart beat in a year?
103563.e: The heart beats about 100,000 times a day. Times 365 days, that makes over 30 million beats.
103563.m: The heart beats over 30 million times a year.

103564.q: About how long does a heartbeat last at rest?
103564.e: At rest the heart beats about 60 to 80 times a minute. So one beat lasts about one second.
103564.m: A heartbeat at rest lasts about one second.

103565.q: About how long does blood take for one full round of the body?
103565.e: Blood flows from the heart through the body and back again. At rest, one round takes about one minute.
103565.m: Blood flows once round the body in about one minute.

103566.q: Why do you bleed even from a small scratch?
a: There are fine blood vessels everywhere in the skin
The skin is filled with blood like a balloon
The heart is right under the skin
Scratches always hit a big vein
103566.e: Fine blood vessels reach almost to the surface of the skin. That is why even a small scratch bleeds.
103566.m: Fine blood vessels lie everywhere just under the skin.

103567.q: About how much blood does a child weighing 30 kilograms have?
103567.e: A person has about 70 to 80 millilitres of blood per kilogram of body weight. At 30 kilograms that is about 2 litres.
103567.m: A child weighing 30 kilograms has about 2 litres of blood.

103568.q: About how many red blood cells does an adult have?
103568.e: About 25 trillion red blood cells float in an adult’s blood. That is a number with 14 digits.
103568.m: An adult has several trillion red blood cells.

103569.q: About how much of your body weight is blood?
103569.e: Blood makes up about 7 to 8 per cent of body weight. At 70 kilograms that is about 5 kilograms.
103569.m: Blood makes up about 7 to 8 per cent of body weight.

103570.q: What is the top layer of the skin called?
103570.e: The skin has several layers. The outermost one is the epidermis.
103570.m: The top layer of the skin is called the epidermis.

103571.q: What is the skin layer directly under the epidermis called?
103571.e: Under the epidermis lies the dermis. It is firm and elastic and contains blood vessels and nerves.
103571.m: The dermis lies under the epidermis.

103572.q: About how many tiny flakes of skin do you lose every minute?
103572.e: The skin constantly sheds old cells. Every minute it is many thousands of tiny flakes.
103572.m: We lose thousands of skin flakes every minute.

103573.q: Which muscles are among the fastest in the body?
103573.e: The muscles that move the eye work lightning fast. They are among the fastest muscles in the body.
103573.m: The eye muscles are among the fastest muscles.

103574.q: How do your eyes move when you read a line?
103574.e: When you read, your eyes jump from word to word. In between they stop very briefly.
103574.m: When reading, the eyes move in small jumps.

103575.q: Can a person turn their eyes independently in different directions like a chameleon?
a: Yes, but only in their sleep
103575.e: In humans, the muscles of both eyes work closely together. A chameleon, on the other hand, can move each eye separately.
103575.m: People can’t turn their eyes separately in different directions.

103576.q: What helps your eyes recover after reading for a long time?
a: Looking very closely at the page
103576.e: When you look into the distance, your eyes have to work less. That way they can relax after reading for a long time.
103576.m: Looking into the distance relaxes the eyes.

103577.q: What moves your eyes up, down and to the side?
103577.e: There are small muscles on each eye. They turn the eye in all directions.

103578.q: What do you do just before you sneeze?
103578.e: Before sneezing you take a deep breath. Then the air is pushed out through the nose and mouth with great force.
103578.m: Before sneezing you breathe in deeply.

103579.q: What do people often say in French when someone sneezes?
103579.e: In French-speaking Switzerland and in France, people often say “À tes souhaits!” after a sneeze. It means roughly “To your wishes!”.
103579.m: In French, people often say “À tes souhaits!” after a sneeze.

a: Yes, for example dogs and cats
103580.e: Many animals with a nose can sneeze. Dogs and cats sneeze, for example, when their nose is irritated.
103580.m: Dogs and cats can sneeze too.

103581.q: Which spice makes many people sneeze when it gets into their nose?
103581.e: Ground pepper strongly irritates the nose. That is why you often have to sneeze when you smell it.
103581.m: Pepper in the nose makes many people sneeze.

103582.q: What colour is a healthy tongue usually?
103582.e: A healthy tongue is usually pink and moist. A thin pale coating is normal.
103582.m: A healthy tongue is usually pink.

103583.q: Can everyone roll their tongue into a tube?
103583.e: Some people can roll up the edges of their tongue, others can’t. That is completely normal.
103583.m: Not everyone can roll their tongue.

103584.q: How fast does a small injury on the tongue usually heal?
103584.e: The tongue has a very good blood supply and is always moist. That is why small bite wounds usually heal within a few days.
103584.m: Small wounds on the tongue heal very fast.

103585.q: About how long is an adult’s tongue?
103585.e: From the throat to the tip, an adult’s tongue measures about 10 centimetres. A large part of it is hidden at the back of the mouth.
103585.m: An adult’s tongue is about 10 centimetres long.

103586.q: In which country did Robert Wadlow, the tallest person ever measured, live?
103586.e: Robert Wadlow was born in 1918 in the state of Illinois in the USA. He lived there all his life.
103586.m: Robert Wadlow lived in the USA.

103587.q: About how tall is Sultan Kösen, the tallest living man (as of 2025)?
103587.e: Sultan Kösen was measured at 2.51 metres. That makes him taller than almost any door.
103587.m: The tallest living man is about 2.51 metres tall.

103588.q: Which vegetable is almost entirely water?
103588.e: A cucumber is about 95 per cent water. That is why it is so refreshing in summer.
103588.m: A cucumber is almost entirely water.

103589.q: About how much of the brain is water?
103589.e: The brain is about three quarters water. That is why drinking is important for thinking too.
103589.m: The brain is about three quarters water.

103590.q: Does the body also get water from food?
103590.e: Fruit, vegetables and soups contain lots of water. So you also take in water when you eat.
103590.m: The body also takes in water with food.

103591.q: What is often left on a sweaty T-shirt after it dries?
103591.e: The water in sweat evaporates and the salt stays behind. That makes white marks on the fabric.
103591.m: Dried sweat leaves white salt marks.

103592.q: How much sweat can a person lose in an hour doing sport in great heat?
103592.e: In heat and with effort, the sweat glands work at full speed. Then you can lose more than a litre in an hour.
103592.m: Doing sport in the heat, you can lose over a litre of sweat an hour.

103593.q: Do you sweat in your sleep too?
103593.e: Even during sleep, the sweat glands release a little sweat. Under a thick duvet often even more.
103593.m: You sweat a little in your sleep too.

103594.q: Which animal has hardly any sweat glands and cools off in mud?
103594.e: Pigs can hardly sweat. That is why they like to wallow in cool mud.
103594.m: Pigs cool off in mud because they hardly sweat.

103595.q: Who usually starts sweating earlier during sport?
103595.e: The bodies of trained athletes learn to cool down faster. That is why they often sweat earlier.
103595.m: Trained athletes usually start sweating earlier.

103596.q: About how much does a person sweat on a normal day without sport?
103596.e: Even without sport, the skin constantly releases a little sweat. On a normal day that is about half a litre.
103596.m: Without sport you sweat about half a litre a day.

103597.q: A child’s heart beats 90 times a minute. How many times does it beat in 2 minutes?
103597.e: You calculate 90 times 2. That makes 180 beats.
103597.m: At 90 beats a minute, a heart beats 180 times in two minutes.

103598.q: You drink 6 glasses of 2 decilitres of water each. How many decilitres is that altogether?
103598.e: You calculate 6 times 2 decilitres. That is 12 decilitres.
103598.m: Six glasses of 2 decilitres each make 12 decilitres.

103599.q: A child loses 1 litre of sweat. How many glasses of 2 decilitres each must they drink to replace it?
103599.e: 1 litre is 10 decilitres. 10 decilitres divided by 2 decilitres makes 5 glasses.
103599.m: For one litre you need five glasses of 2 decilitres each.

103874.q: Which two large joints does the humerus form part of?
103874.e: At the top, the head of the humerus sits in the socket of the shoulder blade; at the bottom the bone forms the elbow joint with the ulna and radius.
103874.m: The humerus connects the shoulder with the elbow.

103875.q: Which two bones join the humerus at the elbow?
103875.e: There are two bones in the forearm, the ulna and the radius. Together with the humerus they form the elbow joint.
103875.m: The humerus, ulna and radius meet at the elbow.

103876.q: What kind of joint does the head of the humerus form with the shoulder blade?
103876.e: The round head of the humerus sits in a socket of the shoulder blade. That is why you can move your arm in almost every direction.
103876.m: The shoulder joint is a ball and socket joint.

103877.q: What is the round upper end of the humerus called?
103877.e: The upper end of the humerus is a half ball covered with cartilage. It glides in the joint surface of the shoulder blade.
103877.m: The head of the humerus is the round end of the bone.

103878.q: Which large shoulder muscle is attached to the side of the humerus and lifts the arm sideways?
103878.e: The deltoid covers the shoulder like a cap and is attached to a rough spot on the shaft of the humerus. It lifts the arm sideways.
103878.m: The deltoid forms the round shoulder and lifts the arm.

103879.q: Which part of the humerus breaks especially often in older people after a fall?
a: The upper end near the shoulder
The lower end at the elbow
The groove of the radial nerve
103879.e: A fracture near the head of the humerus is one of the most common fractures in older people. The bone is often weakened by bone loss.
103879.m: In old age the upper arm often breaks near the shoulder.

103880.q: Which part of the skeleton does the humerus belong to?
103880.e: Arms and hands together form the upper limb. The humerus is its top and longest bone.
103880.m: The humerus is the longest bone of the arm.

103881.q: What else can be injured when the humerus breaks?
a: A nerve that controls the hand
103881.e: An important nerve, the radial nerve, runs around the shaft of the humerus. If it is injured in the fracture, the hand can hang limp.
103881.m: When the upper arm breaks, a nerve can be injured.

103882.q: On which side of the forearm is the ulna?
a: In the middle of the back of the hand
103882.e: If you hold your palm facing forwards, the ulna lies on the inside, on the little finger side.
103882.m: The ulna is on the little finger side.

103883.q: Which part of the ulna forms the hard point of the elbow?
103883.e: The upper end of the ulna forms a strong projection, the olecranon. You feel it when you lean on your elbow.
103883.m: The point of the elbow belongs to the ulna.

103884.q: Which forearm bone is the stronger one near the elbow?
103884.e: The ulna is thick at the top near the elbow and carries the large olecranon there. Towards the wrist it gets narrower.
103884.m: At the elbow, the ulna is the thick bone.

103885.q: Which of the two forearm bones is longer in adults?
a: It differs from arm to arm
103885.e: The ulna reaches from the elbow to the wrist and sticks out above the radius at the top with the olecranon. That is why it is a little longer.
103885.m: The ulna is the longer forearm bone.

103886.q: What is the Latin technical term for this forearm bone on the little finger side?
103886.e: In technical language the bone is called the ulna. The name of the ulnar nerve, nervus ulnaris, comes from it, for example.
103886.m: The forearm bone on the little finger side is called the ulna.

103887.q: How many long bones make up the forearm?
103887.e: The forearm has two long bones: the ulna on the little finger side and the radius on the thumb side.
103887.m: The forearm is made up of the ulna and the radius.

103888.q: Which forearm bone is the humerus’s most important partner at the elbow?
103888.e: The ulna grips the pulley-shaped end of the humerus with a pincer-like notch. This is where the arm bends and straightens.
103888.m: At the elbow, the ulna forms a hinge with the upper arm.

103889.q: Which bump can you feel on the wrist on the little finger side?
103889.e: The lower end of the ulna is called the head of the ulna. It sticks out as a round bump on the back of the hand on the little finger side.
103889.m: The bump on the wrist on the little finger side is the end of the ulna.

103890.q: On which side of the forearm is the radius?
a: On the back of the elbow
In the middle of the palm
103890.e: The radius runs from the elbow to the thumb side of the wrist. There it is wide and easy to feel.
103890.m: The radius is on the thumb side.

103891.q: Which fracture is one of the most common in humans?
a: A broken radius at the wrist
103891.e: When people fall, they often catch themselves with an outstretched hand. The radius often breaks just above the wrist, which is why this fracture is so common.
103891.m: When you fall on your hand, the radius often breaks.

103892.q: Which movement does the radius make possible by turning around the ulna?
a: Turning the hand palm up and palm down
Lifting the arm above the head
Closing the fingers into a fist
Tilting the head to the side
103892.e: When you turn your hand over, the radius rotates around the ulna and crosses it. That way the palm faces up one moment and down the next.
103892.m: The radius turns around the ulna and so turns the hand.

103893.q: Where on the wrist do you usually feel the pulse?
a: On the thumb side above the radius
On the little finger side above the ulna
On the back of the hand above the knuckles
In the middle of the fingertip
103893.e: On the thumb side an artery lies right above the radius. You press it lightly against the bone and feel the pulse.
103893.m: You feel the pulse on the thumb side of the wrist.

103894.q: Which two bones make up the forearm?
103894.e: Two bones lie side by side in the forearm: the radius on the thumb side and the ulna on the little finger side.
103894.m: The forearm is made up of the radius and the ulna.

103895.q: What shape is the upper end of the radius at the elbow?
a: A ring with a big hole
103895.e: The head of the radius is a small disc covered with cartilage. It turns inside a ring-shaped ligament when you turn your hand.
103895.m: The head of the radius turns at the elbow.

103896.q: Which forearm bone forms most of the wrist joint with the carpal bones?
103896.e: The radius is wide at its lower end and carries a joint surface for the carpal bones. The ulna only takes part there through a disc of cartilage.
103896.m: The wrist is formed mainly by the radius.

103897.q: Which muscle is attached to the radius and bends the arm at the elbow?
103897.e: The tendon of the two-headed upper arm muscle (biceps) is attached to a bump on the radius. When it contracts, the arm bends.
103897.m: The biceps pulls on the radius and bends the arm.

103898.q: Why does a knock to the shin hurt so much?
a: The bone lies right under the skin
The bone is hollow and empty inside
There is a big muscle there
103898.e: At the front of the shin, almost no muscle or fat protects the bone. The sensitive outer layer of the bone lies directly under the skin.
103898.m: The front of the shin has hardly any padding.

103899.q: Which bone in the lower leg carries most of the body’s weight?
103899.e: The strong tibia passes the weight from the knee to the ankle. The thin fibula carries only a little.
103899.m: The tibia is the weight-bearing bone of the lower leg.

103900.q: Which ankle bump belongs to the tibia?
103900.e: The lower end of the tibia forms the bony bump on the inside of the ankle. You can feel it clearly under the skin.
103900.m: The inner ankle is the end of the tibia.

103901.q: Which thin bone lies next to the tibia in the lower leg?
103901.e: The lower leg has two bones: the strong tibia and the thin fibula. The ulna and radius are in the forearm.
103901.m: The tibia and fibula make up the lower leg.

103902.q: Which bone does the tibia form the knee joint with?
103902.e: The flat top of the tibia, the tibial plateau, carries the rounded ends of the thighbone. The menisci lie in between.
103902.m: The thighbone and tibia meet in the knee.

103903.q: Where is the kneecap tendon attached to the tibia?
a: At the bump below the knee
In the middle of the fibula
103903.e: Below the knee you can feel a bony bump at the front. That is where the kneecap tendon ends, through which the thigh muscle straightens the leg.
103903.m: Below the knee, the kneecap tendon pulls on the tibia.

103904.q: Why do sporty teenagers sometimes have pain at the bump below the knee while they are growing?
a: The kneecap tendon pulls hard on the growing spot
The skin is too thin there
The knee has too little blood
103904.e: With lots of jumping and running, the kneecap tendon pulls hard on the growth zone of the tibia. That can hurt; it is called Osgood-Schlatter disease.
103904.m: Strong pulling on the growing tibia can cause pain in teenagers.

103905.q: Which protective equipment must football players wear under the rules to protect the shin?
103905.e: Under the rules of football, shin pads are compulsory equipment. They protect the barely padded bone from kicks.
103905.m: In football, shin pads protect against painful kicks.

103906.q: Where is the fibula in the lower leg?
a: On the outside next to the tibia
On the inside next to the tibia
103906.e: The fibula is the thin bone on the outside of the lower leg. It runs parallel to the thicker tibia.
103906.m: The fibula is the slim bone on the outside of the lower leg.

103907.q: Which bone lies next to the fibula in the lower leg?
103907.e: The lower leg has two bones: the thick tibia on the inside and the thin fibula on the outside. The ulna and radius are in the forearm.
103907.m: The lower leg contains the tibia and the fibula.

103908.q: Which of the two lower leg bones is thinner?
103908.e: The fibula is slim and carries only a little weight. The thick tibia carries most of the load.
103908.m: The fibula is the thinner lower leg bone.

103909.q: Is the fibula directly part of the knee joint?
a: No, it lies below the knee
No, it ends at the thigh
103909.e: The head of the fibula is joined to the tibia at the side below the knee. It does not take part in the knee joint itself.
103909.m: The fibula does not reach into the knee joint.

103910.q: Which bony bump does the lower end of the fibula form?
103910.e: You can feel the lower end of the fibula on the outside of the ankle as the outer ankle. The inner ankle is formed by the tibia.
103910.m: The fibula ends at the bottom in the outer ankle.

103911.q: Why can a piece of the fibula be taken to replace bone elsewhere?
a: It carries only a little body weight
103911.e: Because the fibula carries hardly any load, part of it can be removed without making walking difficult. Surgeons use it, for example, to rebuild a jawbone.
103911.m: The fibula carries little weight and can therefore serve as a replacement bone.

103912.q: What is the fibula important for, despite carrying little weight?
a: The stability of the ankle joint
103912.e: With the outer ankle, the fibula and the tibia grip the ankle bone like a fork. That keeps the upper ankle joint stable at the sides.
103912.m: The fibula stabilises the ankle from the outside.

103913.q: What is mainly attached to the thin fibula?
a: Many muscles of the lower leg
The ribs of the rib cage
103913.e: The fibula serves as an attachment for many muscles, such as the fibular muscles on the outside. These lift the outer edge of the foot.
103913.m: Many lower leg muscles are attached to the fibula.

a: At the top of the back of the rib cage
At the front of the chest
At the side of the neck
103914.e: The shoulder blade lies on the upper part of the back of the rib cage. It reaches roughly from the second to the seventh rib.
103914.m: The shoulder blade covers the upper ribs at the back.

103915.q: Roughly what shape is the shoulder blade?
a: Long and round like a tube
103915.e: The shoulder blade is a flat, triangular bone. Its technical name is scapula.
103915.m: The shoulder blade is a flat, triangular bone.

103916.q: Which bone is the shoulder blade joined to by a small joint at the top of the shoulder?
103916.e: At the top of the shoulder, the shoulder blade and collarbone meet in the acromioclavicular joint. In this way the collarbone connects the arm to the trunk.
103916.m: The collarbone connects the shoulder blade to the breastbone.

103917.q: How is the shoulder blade mainly attached to the trunk?
a: By a ball and socket joint on the ribs
By a joint on the spine
103917.e: The shoulder blade has no real bony joint with the ribs or spine. Many muscles hold it in place and let it glide over the rib cage.
103917.m: Muscles hold the shoulder blade in place on the back.

103918.q: What is the spine of the scapula?
a: A bony ridge on the back of the shoulder blade
A tendon on the upper arm
A piece of cartilage in the breastbone
103918.e: The spine of the scapula is a strong bony ridge that runs across the back of the shoulder blade. It ends on the outside at the top of the shoulder.
103918.m: A bony ridge you can feel runs across the shoulder blade.

103919.q: What do the muscles that run from the shoulder blade to the head of the humerus do?
a: They hold the head of the humerus in its socket
103919.e: Four muscles surround the head of the humerus like a cuff. They turn the arm and hold the shoulder joint together. They are called the rotator cuff.
103919.m: Muscles from the shoulder blade hold the shoulder joint together.

103920.q: Which bone forms the shoulder joint together with the upper arm?
103920.e: The head of the humerus sits in the socket of the shoulder blade. Together they form the shoulder joint.
103920.m: The shoulder joint lies between the shoulder blade and the upper arm.

103921.q: What is it called when the shoulder blade sticks out clearly from the back?
103921.e: If a muscle that presses the shoulder blade against the ribs is weakened, its inner edge sticks out like a wing. This is called a winged scapula.
103921.m: A weak muscle can make the shoulder blade stick out.

103922.q: How many bones fuse to form each hip bone during the teenage years?
103922.e: The hip bone is formed from the ilium, ischium and pubis. These three parts grow together in the hip socket during the teenage years.
103922.m: Each hip bone is made of three fused bones.

103923.q: Which part of the skeleton do the two hip bones belong to?
103923.e: Together with the sacrum, the two hip bones form the pelvis. It connects the spine with the legs.
103923.m: The hip bones belong to the pelvis.

103924.q: Which bones together form the pelvic ring?
a: Two hip bones and the sacrum
Two shoulder blades and the breastbone
103924.e: The two hip bones are joined to each other at the front and to the sacrum at the back. That makes a stable ring of bone.
103924.m: The pelvis is a ring of two hip bones and the sacrum.
